speaker: Nick Kokonas
title: Nick Kokonas on Resurrecting Restaurants, Skin in the Game, and Investing
question: In restaurant procurement, why can prepaying major suppliers outperform chasing standard net-60 or net-90 payment terms?
guest: The answer is actually both. About five or six years ago, we realized that if we called the vendors of our more expensive items—meat, fish, wine—and said, 'Hey, we'll make you our exclusive vendor for the next three months, and we'll probably spend about $220,000 during that time; what sort of discount will you give us if we prepay for that?'—almost like a futures contract. So instead of getting net 90 or net 60, which is what every restaurant tries to get, we actually negotiate a discount by prepaying and then truing up afterward. For our big-ticket items, we try to stay a couple months ahead on payments in order to get more favorable terms and better product. It's very rare in the industry. And then for the vendors that are small or won't do that, we keep a capital account so we're always able to cover accounts payable. We're never in a position where if business goes down 30% next week, we can't pay for what we bought four weeks ago.

points.core: Extended vendor payment terms leave restaurants unable to pay past bills during slumps.

points.note: Accept: offering a key vendor quarterly exclusivity and upfront payment (like a futures contract, trued up later) earns lower unit prices. Do not credit: vague mentions of bulk purchasing without upfront prepayment.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Prepaying can outperform extended terms because the discount a supplier will give for cash up front is usually worth far more than the float you gain by paying late.

Restaurants run on thin margins, typically 3–6%, with food at roughly 30% of sales. A 2–5% price cut on major purchases therefore falls almost straight to the bottom line and can lift profit meaningfully. By contrast, holding cash an extra 60–90 days is only worth your cost of capital for that period, often 1–2%. Turning down a 2% discount for 30–60 days of extra float implies an annualized cost well above most borrowing rates.

Suppliers also price risk and financing into long terms. Distributors operate on thin margins themselves and restaurants are a high-default credit category, so net-60/90 often comes with higher prices, or is simply refused. Prepayment removes their credit risk and funds their working capital, which earns you better pricing, priority allocation during shortages, locked-in prices and more negotiating leverage.

The caveat is that this only works if you have the cash (restaurants collect from customers immediately, which helps) and the supplier is financially sound, since prepaying shifts the credit risk onto you.

Restaurants collect customer payments immediately and turn perishable inventory within days, so they rarely need extended float to bridge receivables. Meanwhile, food distributors operate on thin margins in a high-default industry; when asked for net-60 or net-90 terms, they quietly bake their own borrowing costs and credit risk into higher ingredient prices. Prepaying removes that default risk and working-capital strain, unlocking upfront rebates or lower unit pricing—typically 2% to 5%—that compound across rapid inventory turns into risk-free annualized returns far exceeding bank interest on idle cash.

Operationally, upfront payment elevates a restaurant to preferred-buyer status. During supply shortages or seasonal spikes, prepaid accounts receive priority allocation, first pick of fresher, prime-grade proteins and produce, and stronger vendor cooperation on forward commodity price locks. Finally, prepaying enforces financial discipline: whereas long payment terms can mask weak store-level margins behind growing supplier float, paying upfront ensures operations run on genuine cash profitability rather than hidden trade debt.

noweb.answer:
In restaurant procurement, prepaying major suppliers often generates a far higher return on cash than stretching payables to net-60 or net-90. Food distributors and specialty purveyors operate on razor-thin margins while facing high financing costs and steep restaurant default rates; when asked to extend long credit terms, they quietly bake those capital and risk premiums into unit prices. Because restaurants collect customer payments almost immediately and turn perishable inventory within days, a healthy operator already enjoys a fast cash conversion cycle and rarely needs extended supplier float to fund daily operations.

Offering upfront payment eliminates a vendor’s credit risk and working-capital strain, unlocking direct invoice discounts of two to five percent. Giving up sixty days of float for a three percent cost-of-goods reduction yields an annualized, risk-free return above eighteen percent, vastly outperforming interest earned on idle cash while directly widening tight operating margins. Beyond pure math, prepayment elevates a restaurant to preferred-buyer status, securing first pick of peak-quality perishables, priority allocation during supply shortages, and locked-in pricing against seasonal commodity swings.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer: Prepaying can work better because the financing you get from long terms is worth little to a restaurant and usually costs more than it looks. Food inventory turns over in a few days, and customers pay at the table, so a restaurant normally has its cash well before even a net-30 invoice comes due. Stretching to net-60 or net-90 adds little working capital. Distributors know independent restaurants fail often, so they price that credit risk and the cost of carrying receivables into their per-case prices, fees and markups. Paying early shifts the balance the other way. A common 2/10 net-30 discount works out to roughly a 37% annualized return, far more than idle cash earns. Prepayment also gives you leverage to negotiate cost-plus pricing, lock in prices on volatile items like proteins, oils and dairy, and get first allocation when supplies run short. It also makes you a preferred customer, which can mean better service, delivery slots and quality. The trade-offs are less cash on hand and exposure if the supplier fails. So prepay only with stable suppliers, only in amounts your cash reserves can absorb, and only when the discount or price lock is clearly worth it.

In restaurant procurement, extended terms like net-60 or net-90 are rarely free; distributors bake their financing costs and the industry's high default risk directly into food prices. Because restaurants collect customer payments almost immediately, they already operate with a favorable cash conversion cycle and often gain less from supplier credit than they lose in inflated unit costs.

Prepaying major suppliers flips that dynamic. By eliminating credit risk and improving the distributor's own working capital, a restaurant gains leverage to negotiate upfront discounts, sharper everyday pricing, or locked-in rates on volatile commodities like meat, dairy, and produce—savings that flow straight to thin operating margins. Just as importantly, cash-upfront buyers become preferred accounts. When supply chains tighten or ingredients run short, suppliers naturally prioritize reliable, prepaid customers with higher fill rates, fresher inventory, and greater delivery flexibility. Over time, prepaying also reduces administrative friction, avoids credit holds, and turns a transactional vendor relationship into a strategic partnership that consistently outperforms the modest float of stretched payables.
